title: Your Nitnem, for now
hook: a starter Nitnem is an invitation, not a test

segments.voice: Yesterday, how long it takes: an hour or more, and small differences between traditions. Your line was start with one. Did you save the bani you picked? Day one hundred thirty-seven.
screen: `HOW LONG IT TAKES — START WITH ONE.`

segments.voice: Remember being handed a test at school? The paper lands on the desk, face down, and your stomach drops. Pass or fail. A lot of people carry that feeling into religion. They think a daily prayer is a test they'll be graded on, and since they know they'd fail the full version, they never start. Today we finish our ten days on Nitnem, and the most important thing to say is this: a starter Nitnem isn't a test paper. It's more like an invitation card, with your name written on it.
screen: `THE PAPER, FACE DOWN.` → `PASS OR FAIL?` → `AN INVITATION, NOT A TEST.`

segments.voice: Look at where we've been. Nitnem: the daily discipline, morning, evening, night. Japji at dawn, where Guru Nanak says clever thinking won't get you there. Jaap Sahib, galloping praise of the Timeless. The savaiyas: without love, nothing. Chaupai: keep me. Anand: joy, found. Rehras at dusk: put the day down. Sohila at night: the song for sleep. And yesterday, the honest math. So what's a Nitnem for now? For Sikhs who have taken amrit, the full Nitnem is part of their vows, and they keep it. For everyone else walking this path, whether you're a Sikh coming back to practice, someone learning alongside a Sikh partner, or simply curious, the Gurus' own words point to a gentler start. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps describing the Guru as a giver, not an examiner. Again and again the hymns say the Guru's word is like amrit, nectar, something you're offered to drink, not an exam you sit. Japji itself begins by saying the whole thing comes by the Guru's grace, gur prasad, the last words of the Mul Mantar. You didn't earn the invitation. It was sent. So a starter Nitnem might be Japji's first pauri each morning. Or Sohila at night. Or Anand's first stanza with your coffee. Whatever it is, it's said daily, at a time that already exists in your day. And when a day slips, you do what we learned on the breath. You come back.
screen: `TEN DAYS OF THE DAILY BANIS.` · `A VOW FOR SOME, A START FOR ALL.` · `GUR PRASAD — BY THE GURU'S GRACE.` · `SAID DAILY, AT A REAL TIME.` · then, large: `ONE BANI, DAILY.`

segments.voice: Choose one morning bani. Not forever, just for now. Japji's Mul Mantar and first pauri, Jaap's opening, one savaiya, Chaupai's first lines, or Anand's first stanza. Pick it, and picture tomorrow morning: where you'll be, how long it'll take, what you'll read or play. If you're here to learn rather than to pray, choose one to listen to. Then sit with the choice. It's made. The bell holds the time.
Your Nitnem. The daily banis, begun where you are: one bani, said every day, as an invitation, not a test.
Your line: one bani, daily. Tomorrow morning, say or play the one you chose. Just that. Tomorrow we leave the house and go somewhere new. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Amritdhari Sikhs keep the full Nitnem as part of their vows; many other Sikhs and newcomers begin with one bani said daily, such as Japji in the morning or Sohila at night, and add more over time.

what a scholar hears: gur prasad closes the Mul Mantar; grace, not effort, is named first at the Granth's opening.
